passage:
“Chetan bhaiya, is it starting?” Sarika ran into the living room in her blue jersey, a flag painted on each cheek.
“Not yet, sit down,” said her brother. “You’ll sit on the good cushion only if you’re quiet.”
“I’m always quiet,” she said loudly. Nani, folding clothes in the corner, laughed but stayed silent. She supported the other team, and everyone knew it.
When the first ball flew for four, Sarika and Chetan jumped up together, shouting and hugging. Sarika’s voice cracked. “We’re going to win, aren’t we?”
Chetan grinned. “Maybe. But we cheer either way.”
Nani smiled and handed Sarika a glass of water.

qa.q: What was painted on Sarika's cheeks?
qa.a: A flag was painted on each of Sarika's cheeks.

qa.q: Why did Sarika's voice crack when she asked whether they would win?
qa.a: Sarika was so excited and so invested in the match that she was almost out of breath, and she wanted reassurance that her side would win.

qa.q: What did Chetan's reply do for Sarika?
qa.a: Chetan said they cheer either way, which took some of the pressure off winning and kept the fun in the moment.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt about the room cheering for a team she did not support?
qa.a: Nani may have felt amused and outnumbered but warm, since she laughed and gave Sarika water. She stayed quiet about her own side.

grounding: Shows a child in team colours cheering with family, feeling instant belonging and being part of a story.

passage:
My name is Ira, and I’m in Class 4. Our whole class loves the same film hero, and on Fridays we all wear his colour. I wear an orange band on my wrist and a scarf. At lunch we do his dance, and even Rohan, who is shy, joins in.
Only Reena wears green because she likes a different hero. She sits at the edge and eats quietly. Yesterday I asked her to show us her favourite song. She looked surprised, then hummed it, and we clapped.
I like being part of something big. It feels like all of us are in the same story, even when the story has two heroes.

qa.q: Which colour does Ira's class wear on Fridays?
qa.a: The class wears the colour of their favourite hero, and Ira wears an orange band and a scarf.

qa.q: How does Ira feel about being part of the class group?
qa.a: Ira feels happy and proud to belong, saying it feels like everyone is in the same story.

qa.q: What small choice did Ira make that changed things for Reena?
qa.a: Ira asked Reena to show the class her favourite song, which gave Reena a way to join in even though Reena likes a different hero.

qa.q: How might Reena feel sitting at the edge while the others do the dance?
qa.a: Reena may feel a little left out, but not sure, since she eats quietly and looked surprised when Ira asked her. Being invited seems to have been welcome.

grounding: Shows a child loving a film hero with a class, wearing the colour together and feeling belonging in a shared story.

passage: On derby day, Nikita wore her green-and-maroon Kolkata Tigers jersey, two sizes too big, and painted a tiger stripe on each cheek. Their whole lane in Salt Lake had flags on the balconies. When the Tigers scored, the building shook with cheering, and Manjula aunty from downstairs came up banging a steel plate like a drum. Nikita didn't know most of the players' names, but she knew the song. She sang it with the aunties, the uncles and the boys from the corner shop, all of them jumping at once. 'We're Tigers!' she shouted, and for that moment she was, along with everyone else.

qa.q: What did Nikita paint on her cheeks?
qa.a: A tiger stripe on each cheek.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel singing the song with everyone?
qa.a: Joyful and proud, as if she truly belonged to the Tigers crowd, even without knowing the players' names.

qa.q: How could Nikita's family keep derby day friendly?
qa.a: Cheer loudly for the Tigers while staying kind to neighbours who support the other team.

qa.q: What might the derby mean for Manjula aunty?
qa.a: A chance to celebrate with the whole building, banging a plate and sharing the children's excitement.

grounding: A child wears her team's colours and sings with the neighbourhood, feeling instant belonging.

passage:
'Veer Pratap is the best hero ever,' Sumit announced, pulling on his cap with the golden lightning bolt.
'Your hero can't even dance,' said Imran.
'He saved a whole train in Part Two!'
'With a rope. Anyone can do that.'
The other boys on the school steps laughed. Sumit's ears went red. 'You're just jealous because your hero's films are boring.'
Anil held up his own lightning-bolt pencil box. 'I like Veer Pratap too.'
'See?' Sumit grinned. 'Veer Pratap Club. Me and Anil.'
'And me,' said little Gaurav, who hadn't seen any of the films.
Imran rolled his eyes, then smiled. 'Fine. But when the next one comes out, we're all watching it together, and I'm going to laugh at the train scene.'
'Deal,' said Sumit.

qa.q: What was on Sumit's cap?
qa.a: A golden lightning bolt.

qa.q: Why did Sumit's ears go red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and defensive when the boys laughed at his hero.

qa.q: How did the boys turn the argument into something friendly?
qa.a: By agreeing to watch the next film together, so different favourites could still be shared.

qa.q: Why might little Gaurav join the Veer Pratap Club without seeing any films?
qa.a: Gaurav wanted to belong to the group, and loving the same hero is an easy way in.

grounding: Children cheer for a film hero and form an instant club, since loving the same thing gives belonging.

passage: When I was ten, my whole world was the Punjab Panthers kabaddi team. I had the yellow headband, the poster over my bed and every raider's name memorised. On match nights, my friend Pranav and I sat on his roof with a small radio and screamed at every tackle. At school, anyone who wore a Panthers badge was instantly my friend, even kids from other classes I'd never spoken to. Once the Panthers lost the final, and I cried under my blanket. Pranav came over the next morning with two cups of tea and said, 'Next season.' It wasn't really about kabaddi. It was about being part of something loud and yellow and ours. I'm Baljeet, and I still have the headband.

qa.q: What did Baljeet and Pranav listen to the matches on?
qa.a: A small radio, on Pranav's roof.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when the Panthers lost the final?
qa.a: Heartbroken, sad enough to cry under the blanket.

qa.q: How could Baljeet keep the fun of fandom healthy?
qa.a: Enjoy the team and the friendships it brings, while remembering that losses pass and friends like Pranav matter most.

qa.q: What might Pranav's 'Next season' mean to Baljeet?
qa.a: Comfort and loyalty; Pranav shared the love and the loss, and came to say they were still in it together.

grounding: A child's love for a team gives instant belonging and a shared story with friends.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Friday.
Pema came to school today in a yellow team shirt three sizes too big, the number on the back taped where it had torn. It was the morning after the local club won the state football final. Before assembly Pema had a circle of six children around him, acting out the last goal with a lunch box as the ball. Chandrika, who supports the same club, kept shouting "We won! We!" as though she had played. Even Tsering, who usually hangs back, joined the chant. In maths Pema drew the club badge in the margin and wrote OUR TEAM. I let the shirt stay today and asked Pema to write three sentences about the match for English. He wrote seven.

qa.q: What colour was Pema's team shirt?
qa.a: A yellow team shirt, three sizes too big.

qa.q: How can you tell Pema felt proud to be one of the club's fans?
qa.a: He wore the huge shirt, acted out the goal for friends and wrote OUR TEAM, which shows pride and a strong sense of belonging.

qa.q: How did the teacher make good use of Pema's excitement?
qa.a: The teacher let the shirt stay and turned the excitement into writing about the match, so Pema wrote seven sentences instead of three.

qa.q: What might the win have felt like for Tsering, who usually hangs back?
qa.a: Joining the chant probably felt like an easy way in, being part of "we" without having to say much.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a child whose love for a football club gives him instant belonging and a shared story with other fans.
